title: Neither flesh nor blood
hookLine: neither the meat nor the blood reaches Allah, but your mindfulness does (22:37)

lines: A SHEEP, A GOAT, A SHARE IN A COW.
cards: On the morning of Eid al-Adha, in backyards, farms and licensed slaughterhouses around the world, families offer an animal: a sheep, a goat, a share in a cow or a camel.
It's the festival of sacrifice, remembering Ibrahim's readiness to give up his son, and the ram given in his place. For a lot of people, it's the biggest meal of the year.
And in the middle of the surah that sets out these rites, the Qur'an stops to say something that sounds almost like it's undercutting the whole thing.

teach.h: FLESH AND BLOOD DON'T REACH GOD.
teach.b: Verse thirty-seven. Pickthall: "Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him." God doesn't need the meat, or the blood.
The word Pickthall translates devotion is taqwa, which this path has met before: mindfulness of God, a careful awareness that shapes what you do. That's the only part that arrives.

Commentators mention a pre-Islamic custom of smearing sacrificial blood on the Ka'ba's walls, and read this verse as quietly ending that idea: the blood was never the point. So where does the meat go?
A verse just before says it: eat of it, and feed the one who is poor and content and the one who asks.

Many scholars recommend dividing it in three, a third for the family, a third for friends and neighbors, a third for those in need, though they treat that split as good practice rather than a strict rule.
The animal feeds people; the intention goes to God. And this reaches past Eid.
The first hadith in Bukhari's collection says that actions are judged by intentions, and every person gets what they intended. Two people hand over the same envelope at a wedding.
One gives to be seen giving; one gives because they love the couple. The envelopes weigh the same. Only one, in this verse's picture, reaches anywhere at all.
The question isn't how big the gift is. It's what's traveling inside it.

how: Muslims who can afford it offer an animal at Eid al-Adha, often through a local farm, a mosque program or a charity abroad, and share the meat with family, neighbors and people in need.

o: the blood once smeared on the Ka'ba's walls
mindfulness of God, the only part that reaches Him
the meat of the sacrifice shared out at Eid

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: eaten and shared with those in need

s: the Qur'an says the blood of the sacrifice reaches God
22:37 says neither its flesh nor its blood reach God, only the devotion.
the Qur'an tells people to eat from the sacrifice and feed the poor
the verses just before 22:37 say so.
the three-way split of the meat is a strict rule in every school
many scholars recommend it as good practice, not a binding rule.

games.q: it's Eid al-Adha, and your family has offered a sheep. the meat is ready. what does the surah say to do with it?
o: leave it at the Ka'ba as an offering.
eat of it, and feed the poor and the one who asks.
give all of it away and keep none.
games.why: eat, and feed others. God doesn't need the meat, so it goes to people, and only the devotion goes to God.

practice: Think of something you gave recently, or are about to give, money, time, a present, a favor, and ask gently, without judging the answer: who was it for?
If part of it was for being thanked or seen, that's human; set the gift down again in your mind with one clean reason. If you pray, you can offer it to God.

wordCard.voice: Taqwa. Mindfulness of God, the only part of a sacrifice that reaches Him, not the flesh or the blood. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: taqwa, mindfulness of God; Pickthall renders it 'devotion' in 22:37.

carryVoice: Your line: only the heart reaches him. The meat feeds people; the intention travels on. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Their flesh and their blood reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him.
